data: Sirius Satellite Radio launched FM-1 from Baikonur on 2000-06-30 atop a Proton-K. The Tundra orbit (24-hour period, ~25,000 × 35,786 km) at the 63.4° critical inclination keeps each satellite high in the sky over CONUS for two-thirds of every orbit, giving handhelds in urban canyons the elevation angles a geostationary signal can't match. Merged with XM Radio in 2008 to form Sirius XM.
Sirius FM-1 launch (Proton-K, Baikonur) — Gunter's Space Page

Historic satellite-radio constellation in the 24-hour Tundra orbit (~25,000 × 35,786 km) at the 63.4° critical inclination. The three original Sirius FM satellites (FM-1, FM-2, FM-3) each dwelt over CONUS for roughly two-thirds of every orbit, giving urban-canyon receivers elevation angles a geostationary signal couldn't match. Sirius FM-1 launched from Baikonur in 2000 on a Proton-K; FM-2 and FM-3 followed. The company merged with XM Radio in 2008 to form Sirius XM. The Tundra-orbit constellation was decommissioned in 2016, and Sirius XM now operates a fleet of ~7 geostationary satellites.

High-eccentricity orbits at 63.4° critical inclination. Molniya (12-hour, 600 × 40,000 km) — Russian high-latitude comms + Oko/Meridian early warning since 1965. Tundra (24-hour, ~25,000 × ~47,000 km) — Sirius XM Satellite Radio + US SBIRS-HEO sensors.
